citations.cited_for: ESI from sources not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost need not be preserved or produced absent a showing of good cause; backup tapes frequently so classified
quotes: not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost
citations.context: Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b)(2)(B), ESI from sources that are "not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost" need not be preserved or produced absent a showing of good cause by the requesting party.

first_check.quote_check: "not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost" found verbatim in Rule 26(b)(2)(B).
first_check.explanation: The quote and the good-cause mechanism are accurate, but the rule says only that a party 'need not provide discovery' from such sources. It says nothing about relieving a party of preservation. The 2006 Advisory Committee Note says the opposite: calling a source not reasonably accessible does not relieve the party of its duty to preserve, and whether unsearched sources must be preserved depends on the circumstances. So the claim that such ESI 'need not be preserved ... absent a showing of good cause' misstates the rule. The point that backup tapes are often treated as not reasonably accessible is the memo's own commentary; the rule text does not mention backup tapes.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Rule: "A party need not provide discovery of electronically stored information from sources that the party identifies as not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost." 2006 Note: "A party's identification of sources of electronically stored information as not reasonably accessible does not relieve the party of its common-law or statutory duties to preserve evidence."

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The quoted phrase appears in the rule. Rule 26(b)(2)(B) reads: "A party need not provide discovery of electronically stored information from sources that the party identifies as not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost." The rule addresses production only. The 2006 Advisory Committee Note says the opposite of the memo's preservation claim: "A party's identification of sources of electronically stored information as not reasonably accessible does not relieve the party of its common-law or statutory duties to preserve evidence." So saying such ESI "need not be preserved ... absent a showing of good cause" misstates the rule. The good-cause mechanism and the quote are accurate, but the preservation proposition is wrong.

citations.cited_for: Where backup tapes are the only remaining source of relevant data, courts may order restoration at the producing party's expense
citations.context: the Zubulake line of cases from the Southern District of New York, and subsequent decisions in courts across the country, have established that where backup tapes are the only remaining source of relevant data

first_check.correct_citation: Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, 217 F.R.D. 309, 324 (S.D.N.Y. 2003) (Zubulake I); Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, 216 F.R.D. 280 (S.D.N.Y. 2003) (Zubulake III)
first_check.explanation: Zubulake I ordered UBS to restore and produce emails from five sample backup tapes at its own expense, with cost-shifting to be considered afterward. Zubulake III then split restoration costs 75% to UBS and 25% to the plaintiff. So courts may order restoration largely at the producer's expense. The memo leaves out that Zubulake treats backup tapes as the one setting where cost-shifting is appropriate under a seven-factor test. 'Only remaining source' is a simplification: it corresponds to the test's 'availability from other sources' factor. No case or pin is given.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: UBS is also ordered to produce, at its expense, responsive e-mails from any five backups tapes selected by Zubulake. ... the costs of restoring any backup tapes are allocated between UBS and Zubulake seventy-five percent and twenty-five percent, respectively.

citations.authority: Zubulake v. VCB Warburg (sic; real case is Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, Zubulake V)
citations.cited_for: Issuing a hold notice is insufficient; party must take affirmative steps to monitor compliance (written acknowledgments, reminders, audits, hold coordinator)
citations.context: Under Zubulake v. VCB Warburg, 229 F.R.D. 422 (S.D.N.Y. 2004), and Pension Committee of the University of Montreal Pension Plan v. Banc of America Securities, LLC, 685 F. Supp. 2d 456 (S.D.N.Y. 2010), a party must go beyond issuing the notice

first_check.correct_citation: Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, 229 F.R.D. 422, 432-34 (S.D.N.Y. 2004) (Zubulake V)
first_check.explanation: The reporter cite, court, and year are correct, but the party name is wrong: the case is Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, not "VCB Warburg." On substance, the case supports the proposition. Zubulake V holds that it is not enough to notify employees of a litigation hold. Counsel must take affirmative steps to monitor compliance (at 432), including periodically reissuing the hold, communicating directly with key players, reminding them periodically, and instructing employees to produce copies of their files (at 433-34). The document lists written acknowledgments, audits, and a hold coordinator as examples. Those mechanisms are not named in the opinion, but they are a reasonable gloss on its 'reasonable steps' / monitor-compliance rule. The status is driven by the garbled party name, not by any problem with the substance.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: In short, it is not sufficient to notify all employees of a litigation hold and expect that the party will then retain and produce all relevant information. Counsel must take affirmative steps to monitor compliance so that all sources of discoverable information are identified and searched.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. CourtListener lists 229 F.R.D. 422 (S.D.N.Y. July 20, 2004) as "Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC" (cluster 8757285, opinion 8740575), not "VCB Warburg." The reporter, court, and year are correct and the substance is supported. Under the heading "A. Counsel's Duty to Monitor Compliance," the opinion says: "it is not sufficient to notify all employees of a litigation hold and expect that the party will then retain and produce all relevant information. Counsel must take affirmative steps to monitor compliance." The only defect is the garbled party name. Written acknowledgments, audits, and a hold coordinator are the memo's elaboration of that rule, not mechanisms the opinion names.

citations.authority: Pension Committee of the University of Montreal Pension Plan v. Banc of America Securities, LLC
citations.cited_for: Party must go beyond issuing a hold notice and monitor compliance
citations.context: Pension Committee of the University of Montreal Pension Plan v. Banc of America Securities, LLC, 685 F. Supp. 2d 456 (S.D.N.Y. 2010), a party must go beyond issuing the notice and take affirmative steps to monitor compliance.

first_check.explanation: The citation is correct: 685 F. Supp. 2d 456 (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 15, 2010) (Scheindlin, J.). The opinion treats preservation obligations as extending beyond a hold. It faults plaintiffs who did not sufficiently supervise or monitor their employees' collection, holds that an email direction to search was insufficient to constitute a written hold, and calls a custodian's unsupervised search deficient. This supports the paraphrase that a party must go beyond issuing a notice and monitor compliance. Note that Chin v. Port Authority (2d Cir. 2012) later rejected its per se gross-negligence rule for failing to issue a written hold, and it was abrogated in part by the 2015 amendment to FRCP 37(e); this does not affect the proposition.

citations.context: likely protected work product but could be subject to crime-fraud exception arguments if plaintiffs allege knowing concealment.

first_check.explanation: Federal courts hold that the crime-fraud exception can defeat work-product protection as well as attorney-client privilege. The Eleventh Circuit so held in Drummond Co. v. Conrad & Scherer, LLP, 885 F.3d 1324 (11th Cir. 2018). The Fourth Circuit, in In re Grand Jury 2021 Subpoenas, 87 F.4th 229 (4th Cir. 2023), applied the exception to opinion work product but required more than prima facie evidence. One point it leaves out: the exception reaches only materials prepared in furtherance of a crime or fraud, so after-the-fact legal assessments are not automatically exposed.

first_check.explanation: § 1391(b)(1) does make venue proper in a district where any defendant resides, provided all defendants reside in that State. Vantage is the only defendant, so the statute supports the legal proposition. The application is a separate problem: the complaint is filed in the Southern District of Indiana but rests residency on the Fort Wayne headquarters, which is in Allen County and therefore in the Northern District (28 U.S.C. § 94). first_check.explanation: § 1391(c)(2) says an entity defendant resides in any district where it is subject to personal jurisdiction, so it does support the residency proposition in general. But Indiana has more than one federal district, and for a corporation in a multi-district State § 1391(d) is the specific provision: the corporation resides in any district where its contacts would support personal jurisdiction if that district were a separate State. Citing only (c) is incomplete. The factual premise is also flawed. The complaint is captioned in the Southern District of Indiana, Indianapolis Division, yet says Vantage's Fort Wayne headquarters is 'located within this District.' Fort Wayne is the county seat of Allen County, which by statute (28 U.S.C. § 94) is in the Fort Wayne Division of the Northern District. Residency in the Southern District would therefore depend on Vantage's contacts there under § 1391(d).

first_check.explanation: The pre-2026 Quality System Regulation section 21 C.F.R. § 820.90 is titled 'Nonconforming product.' It covers control, review, and disposition of nonconforming product. It does not set the CAPA requirement the complaint cites it for. CAPA procedures were in § 820.100, 'Corrective and preventive action,' which required procedures for investigating the causes of nonconformities. § 820.90(a) mentions only 'a determination of the need for an investigation' of a nonconformance, which is a partial overlap at most. Separately, current eCFR Part 820 is now the Quality Management System Regulation (89 FR 7523, Feb. 2, 2024, effective 2026), so the old section numbers apply only to historical conduct. That is fine here because the alleged conduct was in 2022, but the section number is wrong.

Each manufacturer shall establish and maintain procedures to control product that does not conform to specified requirements... / § 820.100 Corrective and preventive action. (a) Each manufacturer shall establish and maintain procedures for implementing corrective and preventive action.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The pre-2026 21 C.F.R. § 820.90 is headed "Nonconforming product." The CAPA requirement is in § 820.100, "Corrective and preventive action": "Each manufacturer shall establish and maintain procedures for implementing corrective and preventive action," including "(2) Investigating the cause of nonconformities relating to product, processes, and the quality system." The correct provision exists and the section number is wrong, so WRONG_CITATION_REAL_CASE is reasonable. MISCHARACTERIZED would also be defensible.

first_check.explanation: Rule 11(b) makes the certification described: no improper purpose (b)(1), legal contentions warranted (b)(2), and factual contentions supported (b)(3). The complaint is filed in federal court (S.D. Ind.), so the rule applies.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: an attorney or unrepresented party certifies that to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances

citations.context: Veeva Vault is a 21 CFR Part 11–compliant validated system with full electronic signature capability.

first_check.explanation: Part 11 covers electronic records and signatures and requires system validation (section 11.10(a)). The citation correctly names the governing standard. Whether Veeva Vault actually complies is a factual claim about the product, not about the regulation.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: (a) Validation of systems to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and the ability to discern invalid or altered records.
